newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico starts free-market tortilla subsidy system.
newsitem.headline: Mexico starts free-market tortilla subsidy system.

text.p: Mexico launched on Monday the first stage of a more free-market-orientated subsidy system for the industry behind the nation's favorite food - tortillas.

Key to the shake-up is the introduction of electronic cards throughout the entire industry chain in a bid to cut down on subsidy fraud and also to allow tortilla shop owners to buy subsidised wet dough corn or corn flour from their supplier of choice.
Tortillas are pancakes made from wet-dough corn or corn flour and are eaten more widely than bread.
Prices are controlled by the government to ensure that poor Mexicans have access to the staple food. Prices are currenty set in Mexico City at 1.70 pesos per kilo.
Mexico's Trade Ministry announced on Monday it handed over of the first electronic cards to tortilla shop owners in the central state of Aguascalientes.

The cards function like credit cards by storing purchase order information that is punched into hand-held computers. That information is electronically transmitted back to sales companies and also Conasupo, the country's basic foods agency and also the central subsidy point.
Deputy Trade Minister Israel Gutierrez Genaro said the card system will be fully implemented throughout the entire country in coming months.
Gutierrez said the shake-up was in response to an age-old call from the sector to be able to buy corn at market prices and receive direct government subsidies, helping to avoid subsidy fraud.

Mexico's corn flour makers, namely Grupo Industrial Maseca and Grupo Minsa, have long been pushing the government to free up the subsidy system believing they can take market share from wet corn millers, the country's traditional dough makers.
Stage two of the shake-up, once tortilla makers have electronic cards, is to include corn millers in the program, distributing cards to wet millers to buy subsidised corn from Conasupo.
Subsidy ceilings will be set for tortilla makers to make purchases from wet millers and also for wet millers to buy corn from Conasupo.
Stage three of the system will be implemented in early 1998. Tortilla makers will then have a choice of using their purchase ceilings to buy either wet dough or corn flour.

Grupo Minsa, Mexico's second-largest corn flour producer, battled for months to get the government to free up the tortilla subsidies because a Sept. 1996 change in the system effectively capped its sales volumes.

"Through this system, the government not only continued setting the amount of subsidized corn delivered to corn millers but, additionally, limited the monthly sales volume that each of the corn flour producers could sell in every state in Mexico, totally eliminating the natural interactions of market forces in the tortilla industry," Minsa said in a statement.

Minsa, as a result of the sales ceiling system, saw its market share artificially reduced to 24.5 percent in September 1996 from 29.5 percent in August 1996. They company set out on a legal battle against the government's system.
Minsa has since dropped the suit as a result of negotiations with the government and because of start-up of the new system, the company said.

"The program is of great importance for two reasons: Grupo Minsa will have the capacity to compete for a higher market share and the corn flour industry will have the capacity to gain market share away from the tradtional (wet dough) method," Minsa said.
Tortilla makers in nine states -- Quintana Roo, Yucatan, Campeche, Puebla, Morelos, Tlaxcala, Hidalgo, Queretaro and Aguascalientes, will be given electronic cards this month.
In July, the states of Tabasco, Veracruz, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosi, Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, Durango, Zacatecas, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan will be included.

August will see the inclusion of the rest of Mexico's 31 states and Mexico City. The states are Baja California Sur, Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua, Sinaloa, Guanajuato, State of Mexico, Guerrero, Oaxaca and Chiapas.
From September, wet dough corn millers will be given electronic cards. The Trade Ministry said it expects to hand out 38,000 cards in total.
